extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/literary theory of humor; comedy theorists and critics
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical/theoretical account of what makes things laughable and how laughter functions socially; analyzes comic elements in forms, movements, situations, words, and character. Useful for analyzing or producing comic effect in literature, performance, and caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic is strictly human
rubrics_metrics.description: "The comic does not exist outside the pale of what is strictly HUMAN." You may laugh at an animal or an object only insofar as you detect in it some human attitude, expression, shape, or use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: you laugh at an animal only because of some resemblance to man; you may laugh at a hat, but what you are making fun of is the human caprice whose mould it has assumed. This establishes that laughability presupposes human conventions or humanized qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of feeling / emotional detachment
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an "ABSENCE OF FEELING which usually accompanies laughter." The comic requires a spectator's momentary anesthesia of the heart—indifference is its natural environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To laugh you must be a disinterested spectator: pity or strong emotion suppresses laughter. The appeal of the comic is "to intelligence, pure and simple." Practical implication: comic effects work best when the audience's strong emotions are suspended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social/collective nature of laughter (echo/complicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our laughter is always the laughter of a group." Laughter needs an echo or complicity; it is prolonged by reverberation within a social circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many comic effects depend on shared customs and ideas and may not translate across groups. Examples: stories that make a travelling group laugh but not an outsider; fuller theatres produce more uncontrolled laughter. The social function is central to explaining why something makes a particular community laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as social gesture / corrective function
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is a "SOCIAL GESTURE" that, by the fear it inspires, restrains eccentricity and softens mechanical inelasticity; it has a utilitarian aim of social improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson frames laughter as a non-material means by which society discourages eccentric, inelastic behavior and encourages elasticity and sociability. In practice, comic ridicule nudges people to appear what they should be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical inelasticity / automatism
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughable element often consists in "MECHANICAL INELASTICITY" or an "automatism"—a rigidity of movement, thought, or character where living adaptability is expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a runner who falls because muscles continued in momentum; a practical-joke victim acting like a machine; habits that continue despite changed circumstances. Comic effect arises when human responsiveness is replaced by mechanical persistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absentmindedness as comic source
rubrics_metrics.description: A mind that is always thinking of what it has just done and never of what it is doing (absentmindedness) supplies comic matter: "Absentmindedness...has usually fired the imagination of comic authors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absentmindedness can be spontaneous or systematic (e.g., Don Quixote's romantic obsession). It links superficial comic automatism to deeper character-driven comedy; comic authors exploit it as a reliable recipe for comic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin-of-cause naturalness amplifies comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: "When a certain comic effect has its origin in a certain cause, the more natural we regard the cause to be, the more comic shall we find the effect."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comic mishap is funnier when we can trace it to a plausible, intelligible cause (e.g., a man falls because he is intent on a star). The more coherent and reconstructible the cause, the stronger and more expansive the laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internalized rigidity / vice as comic principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Vices that act as a 'ready-made frame'—imposed rigidity brought from without—render characters comic. "The vice capable of making us comic is...that which is brought from without...It lends us its own rigidity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with tragic vices that are fully assimilated into character; comic vices remain recognizably a type (e.g., 'le Jaloux', 'l'Avare') and invite ridicule because the character is unconscious of the ridiculousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic character is unconscious of self
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic person is generally comic in proportion to his ignorance of himself: "The comic person is unconscious...he becomes invisible to himself while remaining visible to all the world."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-awareness reduces comic effect because awareness leads to modification or disguise of the defect. The unconsciousness of the comic defect explains why laughter can correct manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughable physiognomy: imitable deformity / permanent grimace
rubrics_metrics.description: A deformity that may become comic is one "that a normally built person could successfully imitate." A laughable expression is "a unique and permanent grimace" suggesting rigidity and stereotyped action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic physiognomy is not just ugliness but a face suggesting a frozen mechanical action (always laughing, weeping, etc.). The easier it is to imitate and to imagine the person as engaged in a simple mechanical action, the funnier it is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature principle: exaggerate embryonic tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Caricature succeeds when it detects an imperceptible tendency and renders it visible by magnifying it: exaggeration must expose what already exists in embryo, not be aimless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good caricature 'makes his models grimace, as they would do themselves if they went to the end of their tether.' Exaggeration must follow the 'ground plan' of the feature to produce a true caricature rather than arbitrary distortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic opposed to gracefulness rather than beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is to be contrasted more with gracefulness than with ugliness: comic arises where matter resists the soul's mobility, producing rigidity rather than simply ugliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where body or form resists the living, mobile soul and petrifies movements, the effect is comic. Thus analysis of comic effect should look for loss of grace rather than mere ugliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Movements/gestures laughable when they resemble a machine
rubrics_metrics.description: "THE ATTITUDES, GESTURES AND MOVEMENTS OF THE HUMAN BODY ARE LAUGHABLE IN EXACT PROPORTION AS THAT BODY REMINDS US OF A MERE MACHINE."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The clearer and subtler the suggestion of a jointed puppet inside a person—yet still leaving the appearance of life—the stronger the comic effect. Comic artists aim to make the viewer perceive a living person as a mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and imitation produce comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A movement that "is always the same" and repeats at regular intervals becomes laughable because it reveals automatism; imitation of gestures exposes mechanical uniformity and provokes laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Living behaviour should not repeat identically; repetition signals machinery. Thus parody and mimicry, by reproducing repeated gestures, make us laugh by highlighting that element of automatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical interpretation / linking gesture to simple operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Gestures become more laughable when they can be deflected, without altering form, to suggest a mechanical occupation (sawing wood, tugging a bell-rope)—a favourite device of parody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody or context that maps an otherwise human gesture onto a simple mechanical task reveals its mechanistic nature and increases the comic impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic begins as accidental/surface, deepens when internalized
rubrics_metrics.description: Initially the comic may be accidental and superficial (brought about by external circumstance); it penetrates and becomes deeper when the mechanical rigidity is supplied from within the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts/producers of comedy should distinguish between comic caused by external mishaps (slipping, tricks) and comic rooted in character (habitual absentmindedness, ingrained vice), the latter allowing cumulative, systemic hilarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual/comic contrast definitions insufficient without social context
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions reducing the comic to an abstract relation between ideas ('an intellectual contrast', 'a palpable absurdity') do not explain why it makes us laugh; comic must be placed back into its natural social environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay warns against purely logical accounts; to produce or evaluate comic effect, consider social function and practical corrective role, not only formal incongruity.
